newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Palestinians in muted protest on Temple Mount.
newsitem.headline: Palestinians in muted protest on Temple Mount.

text.p: Moslem clerics quelled a brief protest after Friday prayers at al-Aqsa mosque in Jerusalem where extra police were deployed to prevent a renewal of Israeli-Palestinian violence that has killed 73 people.
The mufti of Jerusalem and other religious officials prevailed upon about 500 youngsters to disperse. Israeli police said a few stones were hurled. Palestinians denied it.
Unlike last week police did not storm the mosque complex, Islam's third holiest site, as soon as demonstrations started. Last week they shot dead three stone-throwers.
Police briefly removed thousands of Jewish worshippers from the Wailing Wall below the mosque as a precaution.
More than 3,000 police were deployed in Arab East Jerusalem ahead of prayers.
The Islamic fundamentalist Hamas movement had called for "total confrontations" with Israeli forces and settlers after Friday prayers throughout the West Bank and Gaza.
But Palestinian areas were largely quiet with Palestinian police trying to keep a lid on demonstrations, witnesses said.
Israel has ringed PLO-ruled towns with tanks and prevented Palestinians from travelling in the West Bank and Gaza Strip.

Since last week gunbattles and clashes have claimed the lives of 58 Arabs and 15 Israeli soldiers. The violence was triggered by Israel's opening of an archaeological tunnel beside al-Aqsa complex, a site holy to Moslems and Jews.
PLO officials said President Yasser Arafat had ordered his 30,000-strong police to keep order ahead of U.S.-mediated talks with Israel to restart Palestinian self-rule.

The decision to hold the talks on Sunday at the Erez crossing between Gaza and Israel was the main achievement of an emergency White House summit to end the violence last week. Israelis have called the meeting with President Bill Clinton a success, Palestinians deemed it a flop.
Israel's new right-wing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu appealed to Palestinians not to lose hope.

"I ask you, don't go into mourning. Don't lose hope," Netanyahu said on Israel Channel One television's Arabic service in an address to Palestinians on Thursday night. "This is an opportunity for a fresh start for the peace process."
Israel's delayed troop redeployment in the West Bank town of Hebron will top the Erez talks, which may be attended by U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher.
In Hebron, plainclothes Palestinian police mingled with crowds urging calm when Israel briefly lifted a curfew to allow shopping, witnesses said.

The Palestinian police have not yet deployed in Hebron, the last major Palestinian town still under occupation. But witnesses said members of the force, some with pistols and two-way radios, were trying with Israel's knowledge and approval to prevent youths from confronting the Israeli army.
A senior Israel official who returned with Netanyahu on Thursday from the White House summit said a stabilisation period of some 90 days was needed after the clashes.
